Says prospects compare against incumbent tools or building in-house. Cites Workato in CALL-001 and MuleSoft in CALL-004.
Covers integration effort and mentions there is no one-click SAP connector.

Mentions usage/seat assumptions, surprise overages and hidden seat charges.
Ownership is framed only as wanting clear run history and team-owned queues. It does not say prospects lack internal capacity or doubt that a platform reduces maintenance.

answer.summary: Across these calls, the biggest hesitation is commercial: prospects repeatedly worry about price, annual commitment, usage/seat assumptions, and surprise overages or hidden services. The next most common blockers are governance and approval complexity, security/compliance requirements, and whether the first use case is scoped tightly enough to prove value before asking for broad rollout. Many also hesitate because the workflow ownership model, auditability, integrations, data residency, and AI controls are not yet specific enough for them to trust the proposal.

answer.summary: Across these calls, the most important capabilities are observability/control features: run history with status, inputs, outputs, retries and approvals; team-level exception handling; version/change history; and audit/export into customer tools. Prospects also repeatedly care about governance and security controls — SSO/SCIM, audit logs, retention, residency, no-training commitments, and AI that can be disabled or tightly constrained — plus integration quality, especially validating the actual required operations for core systems rather than just having a connector logo. This is an inference from the calls, not an explicit commitment by the prospects, and the repeated signals are the same across industries: reduce manual coordination, make ownership visible, and keep risky changes and exceptions reviewable.
